segments.text: 1991 ends one order, not history itself — European integration deepened and expanded, but the Balkans experienced brutal wars, NATO enlarged amid controversy, terrorism reshaped security policy, and the 2008 financial crisis exposed real weaknesses in European economic governance.
Former communist states moved toward market economies and multiparty systems with genuinely uneven results, while Russia itself faced severe economic and political upheaval through the 1990s.
German reunification (3 October 1990)

, though technically just before the syllabus’s nominal starting point, is essential background: Western leaders deliberately sought to embed the larger reunified Germany firmly inside NATO and European institutions.
The breakup of Yugoslavia produced wars in Croatia, Bosnia, and later Kosovo, with ethnic cleansing and mass atrocities that seriously challenged hopes for a peaceful post-Cold War Europe. The
Maastricht Treaty (1992)

created the European Union and set a path toward monetary union, with the euro introduced for electronic use in 1999 and notes and coins entering circulation in 2002; later enlargement brought many former communist states into the EU.
NATO enlargement

eastward was viewed by supporters as consolidating security and democracy, and increasingly viewed by Russian leaders as a strategic challenge — a genuine and continuing point of dispute worth presenting from both perspectives.
European states cooperated with the United States after
, especially in Afghanistan, but the
2003 Iraq War
produced major divisions within Europe itself; terrorist attacks in European cities further shaped domestic security policy through this period. The
2008 global financial crash
led to recession, bank rescues and sovereign-debt problems, and the subsequent
Eurozone crisis
exposed real tensions between shared monetary policy and continued national fiscal responsibility.

The post-2008 sovereign-debt crisis exposing tension between shared currency and national fiscal policy.

segments.text: Preparation Checklist

items.text: Build the topic around four transformations: post-communist transition, German/European integration, Balkan conflict, and economic-security challenges after 2001; keep material within the syllabus endpoint of 2012 unless a question explicitly invites later developments.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why should 1991 be understood as the end of one European order rather than the end of European conflict and instability altogether?”

segments.text: Common Confusions to Avoid

items.text: Do not begin the topic in 1991 while ignoring German reunification in 1990; it is essential background.
Do not treat EU and NATO enlargement as the same process; they have different purposes and membership rules.
Do not assume the end of the Cold War ended nationalism or war in Europe; the Balkan wars show otherwise.

segments.text: Easy Revision Points

items.text: Germany formally reunified on 3 October 1990; the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
The breakup of Yugoslavia produced wars in Croatia, Bosnia and later Kosovo.
The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992; the euro entered circulation in 2002.
The 2008 financial crisis and Eurozone sovereign-debt crisis exposed weaknesses in European economic governance.
Treat 1991 as the end of one order, not the end of history: integration deepened, but nationalism, war, terrorism and financial instability all persisted afterward.

Present NATO enlargement’s contested significance from both the Western-security and Russian-strategic-challenge perspectives, since this remains a genuinely disputed point relevant to later European security debates.
